source_document.body:
Sanofi’s Infilbray is designed to cross the blood-brain barrier, allowing the drug to prevent the toxic buildup of disease-causing lipids in the brain.
The FDA has signed off on Sanofi’s oral drug venglustat to treat patients with type 3 Gaucher disease over a certain weight.
The once-daily pill, to be sold under the brand name Infilbray, is the first medicine approved by the agency that targets the neurological symptoms of the disease, according to the FDA’s announcement of the approval Wednesday evening.
Type 3 Gaucher disease (GD3) is a rare disorder driven by a deficiency in a certain enzyme, leading to the toxic buildup of a specific lipid inside cells. This disease not only leads to enlarged organs and anemia but also affects the brain, triggering a variety of neurological symptoms that include abnormal eye movements and seizures.
Designed to cross the blood-brain barrier, Sanofi’s Infilbray is intended to address GD3 by tamping down production of the disease-causing lipids, in turn reducing their accumulation in cells across the body, according to the FDA. The blood-brain barrier protects the brain from harmful substances but has also posed a challenge to drug developers looking to deliver their therapies into the organ.
In the Phase 3 LEAP2MONO study , which enrolled 43 patients, Infilbray outperformed enzyme replacement therapy (ERT)—the current standard of care—at improving neurological outcomes at 52 weeks, hitting the trial’s primary endpoint, according to a February readout . Infilbray was also just as good as ERT at improving the non-neurological manifestations of GD3, such as spleen and liver volumes and hemoglobin levels.
The FDA previously granted Infilbray breakthrough therapy, rare pediatric disease and fast-track designations.

“We have been able to treat the systemic manifestations of Type 3 Gaucher disease, while the neurological manifestations remained beyond the reach of available therapies,” trial investigator Pramod Mistry, director of the Yale Lysosomal Disease center and Gaucher Disease Treatment Center, said in a prepared statement on Wednesday.
Sanofi already has one approved therapy that addresses the systemic but not neurological manifestations of GD3: the ERT Cerezyme . The company also owns the enzyme inhibitor Cerdelga , which is indicated for a different type of Gaucher disease.
Aside from GD3, Sanofi is also developing venglustat for Fabry disease, another rare lysosomal storage disorder. Results from the Phase 3 PERIDOT study in February found no significant benefit on neuropathic and abdominal pain, missing the study’s primary endpoint, but the pharma has an ongoing Phase 3 study of the drug’s effects on left cardiac ventricular mass index in adults with the disease.
In a handful of other indications, however, venglustat has hit apparent dead-ends. In 2022, Sanofi discontinued a mid-stage study for another group of rare, inherited lysosomal disorders called GM2 gangliosidosis following disappointing data, and a year earlier, the pharma canned a Phase 2/3 trial for kidney disease and a Phase 2 test in Parkinson’s disease, also because of underwhelming efficacy. Venglustat is no longer in development for any of these indications, according to Sanofi’s pipeline page .

Tiny House Aigoual Creates a Light-Filled Oasis in Less Than 250 Square Feet
16 photos
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois
The idea of an oasis-like private sanctuary filled with natural light typically brings to mind the kind of spacious, luxurious XL tiny homes that are so popular in the US, but it doesn’t necessarily have to be so. French artisans are experts at making even the most compact wooden mobile homes look and feel extra luminous, even with simple techniques.
Tiny house Aigoual looks a bit different than its sister tiny homes from the same builder, the Occitania-based Mon Reve en Bois. It proudly shows off the same traditional French house silhouette with a double-pitched roof, elegant windows, and natural timber cladding, yet the eye immediately goes to the silvery aluminum trims and rooftop – an unusual, unexpected style element that adds an urban edgy without clashing with the rustic aesthetic.
It makes tiny house Aigoual pop – you’ll notice it among a crowd of wooden tiny homes, and you’ll surely remember it afterwards. The discrete color of the aluminum trims, and the muted shine, complement the natural tone and texture of the Douglas pine exterior beautifully, staying in line with this builder’s minimalist, artisan aesthetic that bans anything artificial or flashy.
This isn’t just any regular timber, either. The Douglas pine and spruce are sourced exclusively from local, sustainably-managed woods in Occitania. This local wood is specifically chosen for its highly resinous composition that makes it naturally resistant to insects, the elements, and weather damage overall. It’s also easy to maintain long-term, not to mention the beautiful natural texture and tone that make almost every French tiny house so special.
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois Relying on local, sustainably-sourced timber is one of the sustainable practices that this French builder strives to incorporate in the workshop’s everyday activity. They also recycle all the wood waste resulting from the building process, and try to opt for as many eco-friendly components as possible. Aside from the construction process itself, they encourage customers to opt for the autonomous kits that turn these rustic mobile homes into self-sufficient abodes.
A regular autonomy kit from this builder includes a solar energy system adapted to the size of the house, a waterless toilet, and a water storage tank plus the filtration system, but options go as far as a solar-powered water heater and a separate, exterior waterless toilet. A wider range of options means that tiny home owners with different needs and budgets can find the best way to fit these off-grid solutions into their new lifestyle – better for them and for the environment.
Size-wise, this particular model stays within the typical dimensions of wooden homes on wheels built in France, but the one-loft layout allows for generous accommodation. A standard 2.5-meter (8 feet) width coupled with less than 7 meters (23 feet) in length would lead you to believe that there’s not too much flexibility inside this home on wheels, yet you’d be surprised to find out not only that it can accommodate four people, but that it’s extra bright and airy as well.
From the outside, you can spot the big, romantic porthole-windows that bring more light to this tiny house as well as adding a touch of whimsy. You’ve surely seen tiny homes with one porthole added to the lounge or the loft bedroom as a style statement, but models with three rounded windows (aside from the regular ones) are quite unusual.
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois Tiny house Aigoual has one in the lounge, right above the sofa, one in the loft bedroom above, and a third one in the kitchen, close to the main entrance. The visual effect is lovely, and nobody will complain about even more natural light finding its way to this timber interior. Strategically-placed windows along with a four-meter (13 feet) height are a classic solution for enhanced luminosity and airiness in a tiny house, and the portholes are the cherry on top.
In this space-efficient layout, the solid, custom-crafted staircase that leads to the main bedroom becomes the central part of the house, with the compact kitchen and bathroom on one side, and the open lounge on the other side. This placement creates separation between the two areas without blocking the flow – in other words, there’s balance between unobstructed movement around the house and the need for privacy.
Small, basic kitchens are the norm when it comes to French tiny homes. You’ll rarely see an American-style family kitchen with premium countertops, full-size appliances, and classic cupboards in one of these wooden homes. Instead, countertops are plain and compact, storage typically includes a couple of lower cabinets plus floating shelves, and small-to-medium appliances that are almost never seamlessly incorporated into the furniture.
These small kitchens are almost a perfect expression of the inherent bohemian spirit of French tiny homes – imperfect, but full of charm. In Tiny house Aigoual, placing the kitchen to one end of the layout could make it seem even smaller, cramped, and dark, but the builder has cleverly added one of the portholes here, for added luminosity, as well as choosing full glazing for the main entrance, to bring in even more light.
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois The shape and design of the upper cupboards were also adapted to the limited space available, and an extra-small loft space above offers additional storage. Overall, this kitchen is so small that the bathroom fits right next to it, yet it’s fully equipped with all the essential appliances for permanent accommodation. The same applies to the bathroom, which has just enough floor space for a conventional toilet, an enclosed shower cabin, and a slim vanity with a tiny sink.
Tiny Aigoual’s lounge is intended for multi-functionality. Instead of a conventional sofa, it’s furnished with a custom-crafted bench, another bespoke feature that makes each of these wooden tiny homes unique. Apart from comfy seating, this bench can be turned into a two-person bed, and it also provides generous storage in the form of built-in drawers. With large windows on each side, as well as a beautiful porthole right above, this open lounge enjoys maximum light.
By avoiding bulky furniture and by placing windows in just the right areas, all around the house, this French builder has turned what could be considered a compact mobile home into a welcoming, peaceful oasis that looks much more spacious than its actual size. Natural light seems to embrace those inside wherever they are, including the loft bedroom.
This 6-square-meter (64.5 square feet) bedroom comes with the advantages that only bigger tiny house lofts typically offer. Most impressive: two large windows flanking the bed, plus a large round window on the wall behind the bed. Add to this ample walk-around space, and you get a loft that feels deliciously spacious, not to mention the quality and durability of its floor and walls, compared to cheaper versions.
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois A mid-height safety wall adds just the right amount of privacy while keeping this bedroom as light-filled as the rest of the house, an oasis within an oasis. The sturdy staircase also contributes to the overall high comfort level, especially in the long run, compared to ladders or hybrid staircases. Plus, the staircase was crafted to hide ample storage space beneath a few doors, a more elegant solution than the standard open compartments.
From the delicate touch of the aluminum trims to the off-grid features and whimsical portholes, Aigoual stands out among French tiny homes – an excellent option that can house up to four people, providing comfortable and sustainable long-term accommodation.

M&A returned to the contract logistics sector over the past 24 hours as US-based Neovia Logistics was snapped up by Logisteed and Turkey’s Ekol Logistics was sold to Arvato.
Japanese freight forwarder and 3PL Logisteed is to acquire pure-play contract operator Neovia Logistics, creating a platform for Logisteed to expand into the North American market.
Neovia, which began life as the in-house logistics arm of US heavy equipment manufacturer Caterpillar, has been owned by a group of private equity funds – Oaktree Capital Management, Ares Management, and Vector Capital – since 2022, and has been through series of ownership changes since it was carved-out of its parent company in 2012.
Financial details of the transaction have not been disclosed. However, Neovia’s 2025 adjusted revenues were recorded at $589m, with EBITDA of $66m, and has a current roster of just under 6,000 employees.
According to Logisteed, there will be little overlap between the activities of the two companies, with 54% of Neovia’s revenue coming from North America, 40% from Europe and just 6% from Asia-Pacific. In contrast, Logisteed earns 71% of its turnover from Asia-Pacific, 19% from Europe, and 10% from North America.
However, Logisteed, in which Japan Post acquired a 20% stake last year, is a far bigger enterprise, recording revenue of around $6.2bn in calendar year 2025.
It said new markets and new supply chain capabilities were a key feature of the acquisition.
“Logisteed customers gain deeper North American and European contract logistics capabilities, while Neovia customers gain access to Logisteed’s APAC network and broader transportation and forwarding capabilities,” it said.
It added that shippers would be offered “a more comprehensive suite of integrated supply chain solutions by combining both companies’ expertise in contract logistics with Logisteed’s forwarding, transportation, and other functions.”
Neovia chief executive Mike Fahy said: “Today marks the start of an exciting new chapter for Neovia, our customers, and our people.
“Logisteed shares our commitment to operational excellence and to the people who deliver it every day, and we are excited to continue our journey together – our leadership team will remain in place, and our priorities do not change,” he added.
The deal is expected to close at the end of the first quarter next year.
Elsewhere, German supply chain management and e-commerce logistic provider Arvato announced today it had agreed to acquire Turkey’s Ekol Logistics – the remaining domestic operation, not sold to Danish ferry operator DFDS is early 2025.
Arvato, part of Germany’s Bertlesmann Gourp, said the deal would expand its Turkish footprint to 1.2m sq metres of logistics space across 26 warehouses, and “further strengthen Arvato’s position in fashion and consumer electronics logistics” plus “establishes a significant presence in healthcare logistics and provides an attractive entry point into the FMCG sector”.
Frank Schirrmeister, Arvato CEO, added: “By combining Arvato’s international network with Ekol’s strong local platform, we are creating new opportunities for growth, greater operational flexibility, and enhanced supply chain performance for our clients.
“At the same time, the transaction underscores our ambition to invest in markets where we see long-term growth opportunities and where we can create tangible value for our clients,” he added.
The deal value was undisclosed, and completion remains subject to regulatory approval.

B-21 Raider Closer to Becoming the World's First Sixth-Gen Bomber After Weapons Release Test
19 photos
Photo: Northrop Grumman
Quickly and carefully, the United States is moving closer and closer to becoming the first nation on the planet to operate a sixth-generation aircraft. That would be the B-21 Raider nuclear bomber presently being developed by defense contractor Northrop Grumman for the U.S. Air Force (USAF).
Just four years after it was first presented at the company's facilities in Palmdale, California, the stealth nuclear bomber reached another important development milestone after executing its first-ever weapons release test. In other words, it proved it can drop bombs, which will be its main mission once it becomes operational.
The test was announced by Northrop Grumman earlier this month, but without any details on what was actually done or what the objectives were. We're only told the test showed the B-21’s ability to carry and employ combat power.
With this out of the way, the defense contractor is now accelerating the development of the plane, as it still plans to deliver the first operational example to the Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota as soon as next year.
As per the limited details on the design available at the time of writing, the Raider has been imagined so that it can deploy a variety of weapons, from nuclear and conventional bombs to missiles of a wide variety.
Up to 20,000 pounds (9,100 kg) of munitions can be transported at a given time, and the design is made in such a way as to allow the accommodation of weapons that have not yet been developed.
The announcement concerning the weapons release test comes about half a year after we were told the Raider had successfully performed aerial refueling tests, something that truly unlocks its capability of reaching any point on the planet without having to land.
In the meantime, we were also informed that the plane had demonstrated outstanding stealth performance, but no details on what that means have been provided. Lifetimes of fatigue testing have also been completed, months ahead of schedule.
When fully operational, the Raider will eventually replace two of the three airplanes that currently form the trio of nuclear-capable bombers, the B-1B Lancer (introduced in 1986) and the B-2 Spirit, which has been in the sky since 1997. The third plane, the B-52 Stratofortress, will fly alongside the Raider into the 2050s, effectively becoming the world's first aircraft to still be operational a century after its first flight.
When it comes to capabilities, the information released so far paints the picture of a potent machine. Powered by a pair of Pratt & Whitney PW9000 non-afterburning turbofan engines rated at 27,000 pounds of thrust each, the bomber will be capable of flying at subsonic speeds of Mach 0.8 (614 mph/988 kph), and will fly at max altitudes of 50,000 feet (15,000 meters).
The aircraft will first be deployed at the Ellsworth Air Force Base, which will also be the place where Raider pilots will train. Later down the line, airbases Whiteman in Missouri and Dyess in Texas will accommodate it as well. There is word of the USAF needing a fleet of up to 100 of these bombers.
The designation of the stealth plane follows the USAF tradition, with B designating a bomber, and the number 21 the century the plane was born. The word Raider references Lt. Col. James 'Jimmy' Doolittle and his crew of 80 airmen who flew 16 B-25 Mitchell medium bombers on a raid on Tokyo and other cities on the island of Honshu in the wake of the Pearl Harbor attack.

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine plans to double its drone supplies and more than triple its long-range strike capabilities next year, according to Ukraine’s defense minister, as Kyiv presses ahead with its long-range strike campaign despite the Pentagon’s criticism of attacks deep inside Russia.
Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara made the announcements Tuesday at a press conference after the 37th meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group at NATO headquarters in Brussels.
“There are prospects in this, and we are only getting started,” he said.
A day later, the British government said in a statement that it will send Ukraine more than 1,000 long-range strike drones, some able to fly more than 620 miles (1,000 kilometers), in a roughly $342 million (£260 million) package.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to announce the offer Thursday in Berlin at a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing” of Ukraine supporters, where U.S. special envoys Jared Kushner and Steven Witkoff are expected to brief European leaders on peace negotiations.
Ukraine is forging ahead with its long-range strike campaign with support from European partners, despite Washington’s request to prioritize front-line defense and associated midrange strikes instead.
Khmara told the EU Foreign Affairs Council that drones will make up more than half of Ukraine’s weapons needs in 2027. At the press conference, he said 62% of funding should go to drones, including first-person-view, middle-strike, deep-strike and logistics drones.
U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner (center) and Steven Witkoff (right) are welcomed by Günter Sautter (front), the Federal Chancellor’s advisor on foreign and security policy, at the meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing” at the Federal Chancellery in Berlin on Nov. 19, 2026. (Bernd von Jutrczenka/picture alliance via Getty Images)
“While the public conversation focuses on the spectacle of deep strikes designed to incur pain on the Russian population, our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the front line,” Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby said in his opening remarks to the meeting.
Such strikes, “especially those that target civilian infrastructure, such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public’s resolve and the Kremlin’s own willingness to escalate,” he said.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius responded in a press conference after the meeting, stating that faulting strikes on “strategic military and military use targets” in Russia is “quite a stupid thing, I think.”
“We should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on civil energy, water and heater infrastructure in Ukraine,” Pistorius said.
Colby left the meeting shortly after his own remarks, before the press conference, according to two sources cited by The Telegraph , one of whom said he did not stay for Khmara’s classified briefing.
Colby “definitely appeared more on the side of Russia than on the side of Ukraine,” a German source told the publication.
Colby’s remarks follow pressure from the Trump administration on Kyiv to spare Russian refineries .
Colby also said that strikes that target “Russia’s warmaking machinery can also help contribute to slowing Russia’s advance on the front lines” and that Ukraine should not “be forced to fight with its hands tied behind its back.”
Further support from European allies announced at the meeting included a pledge by Germany to buy jointly produced middle-strike and deep-strike drones, and a promise from Norway to set aside $300 million to buy Ukrainian drones, according to a Defense Ministry readout .
British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said at the same press conference that deep strikes have “helped to degrade Putin’s war machine, buying time and saving lives.” He also said Colby’s attendance in person was “a further demonstration of U.S. commitment and involvement.”
Britain’s new drones will let Ukraine target “military production facilities and other legitimate military targets far behind the front lines,” according to a government statement .
“It’s not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war,” Britain’s Streeting said.

GM Canada's Oshawa Assembly Plant Hits 600,000th Chevrolet Silverado Production Milestone
17 photos
Photo: GM Canada
600,000 trucks in five years isn't a bad result for a factory that was previously found itself on the brink. The Oshawa complex resumed truck production in November 2021, and the Ontario-based facility is celebrating another milestone as it prepares for nearly CAD 500 million in additional investment for the next-generation Chevrolet Silverado HD and GMC Sierra HD.
More than 600,000 trucks in the span of 60 months is a tremendous result, working out to 120,000 vehicles annually. GM's Canadian subsidiary hasn't provided a year-by-year production breakdown, yet the cumulative figure shows how quickly a once-doomed plant can re-establish itself authoritatively.
Said 180-degree turn was not guaranteed, though, albeit North America has a big appetite for large trucks. Back in November 2018, the Detroit-based automaker made it clear that Oshawa would end vehicle production by December 2019. Instead, the company would have converted Oshawa to stamping, subassembly, and less important manufacturing activities.
No fewer than CAD 170 million supported the downgrade, yet a reversal came in November 2020. The Big G announced that full-size truck production is the name of the game, retooling the facility and recruiting workers as it prepared for a two-shift operation. The reopened assembly line started churning out Silverados on November 10, 2021, creating 1,800 new jobs at the plant while supporting thousands more throughout Canada's automotive supply chain.
The Silverado program is the latest chapter of a story that started in November 1953. Over the years, Oshawa has built everything from lousy Pontiacs and Buicks to the Chevrolet Camaro. During WWII, tanks and machine guns were the norm. The Cadillac XTS and Chevrolet Equinox were assembled there as well. Before the 2019 shutdown, it specialized in Silverado and Sierra pickups.
Photo: GM Oshawa accommodates both light- and heavy-duty truck production alongside stamping, subassembly, and aftermarket parts production. Regarding the latter, June 2026 saw the plant pass 1 million aftermarket parts produced since the 2021 restart. Come December 2026, the Canadian facility will make the switch to the 2027 model year Chevrolet Silverado HD, new diesel engine and all.
The L6P turbo diesel, which is the largest one yet at 8.3 liters, comes from the DMAX plant in Brookville, Ohio. As for the lesser L8S gasoline V8, that one is assembled at Tonawanda Propulsion in Buffalo, New York. While both mills are neat in their own ways, the Duramax is the one to have for effortless towing.
Beyond the revised engine lineup, the 2027 model year Silverado HD further prides itself on new trailering, braking, and steering technologies. Going forward, those CAD 500 million will be invested over the next three years. The investment can be split between 343 million for truck production and various additional improvements, and 144 million to bring the next-generation Sierra HD.
The investment in question is connected to St. Catharines Propulsion, where more than CAD 900 million has been committed for V8 and transmission production. Said programs support the full-size truck and SUV lineup across North America, meaning that engines and transmissions from St. Catharines Propulsion will eventually be used by the Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon, and Escalade.
Five years ago, the question was whether Oshawa would build vehicles again. Today, making preparations for another generation of trucks is a win for both the largest automaker of the Detroit Big Three and the approximately 3,100 workers operating there on a two-shift schedule. Desert Sand LS6 Is a Holy Grail 1970 Chevy Chevelle in a Very Rare Color
14 photos
Photo: Patrick Glenn Nichols Musclecar Barn Finds/YouTube
Introduced in 1963 as Chevrolet's first full-size car, the Chevelle remained on the assembly line through 1977. Like most intermediates of the era, the Chevelle joined the muscle car wars. It also spawned the most powerful production car of the era.
The latter arrived for the 1970 model year with a 454-cubic-inch (7.4-liter) powerplant under the hood. It's called the LS6 and produced a whopping 450 horsepower thanks to a four-barrel Holley carburetor and heavy-duty internals. Torque was just as impressive at 500 pound-feet (678 Nm).
The mill also found its way into the Monte Carlo and the Corvette, but it was short-lived. It returned in 1971 in the Corvette sports car only, this time around with a detuned rating. When it comes to the Chevelle, the LS6 version is a one-year-only model.
Chevrolet sold over 400,000 Chevelles in 1970, but only 4,475 units are said to have been ordered with the mighty LS6. The number includes about 500 El Camino pickups , so we're looking at under 4,000 units with the two-door hardtop and convertible body styles (the drop-tops are super rare).
Although there's no shortage of LS6 vehicles on today's classic car market, only a tiny fraction of them still have numbers-matching engines under the hood. According to Chevelle expert Patrick Glenn Nichols, only two to three out of 10 vehicles can still brag about that. We're probably talking about only a few hundred cars. This Desert Sand hardtop is one of them.
Found in Olathe, Kansas, this Chevelle was recently removed from storage to be checked and endorsed by Mr. Nichols. And it's quite the noteworthy Chevelle. In addition to the numbers-matching drivetrain , it also has the desirable four-speed manual transmission, while the color combo is quite rare.
Specifically, it has a Desert Sand exterior with no vinyl top and a saddle interior. The combo was reportedly ordered on less than 3% of the LS6-fitted Chevelles, according to the official registry. That's fewer than 130 examples made, with the number of actual survivors being much smaller.
Unlike the very similar LS6 we saw cross the block back in 2021 , this Chevelle is not Concours-ready. Although it looks pretty good inside and out, it has a few issues that need to be addressed, mostly in the mods department. Patrick found a modern power steering unit, an aftermarket fan, and incorrect front seatbelts.
These items didn't stop him from endorsing the car, though. After all, it's a mostly original LS6 with rare matching-number drivetrain components. It also has two build sheets. But these issues will need to be addressed in order to bring this Chevelle back to factory-correct status.
Mr. Nichols says that the Chevelle may change hands soon, but there's no info on how much the current owner wants for it. I can definitely say that it's a six-figure classic , but I wouldn't bet on it going for over $200,000. But it could become a quarter-million-dollar collectible with a bit of work. Aptera (SEV) has finished building its first solar electric vehicle for a paying customer. It’s going to Martin Hartono, the startup’s No. 1 “Accelerator” investor, and it’s being exported out of the US.
It’s a real milestone for a company that has pushed back its delivery dates since 2022. And it comes a week after Aptera reported $9.2 million in cash against the roughly $25 million it says it needs to start series production.
A matte black Aptera for Accelerator #1
Aptera announced today from its Carlsbad, California headquarters that it completed what it calls its first production solar electric vehicle. The car is finished in “Noir,” a matte black exterior, and was built for Accelerator #1.
Accelerators are investors from Aptera’s community funding program, where delivery priority goes to whoever invests the most . So the first customer car went to the biggest check.

Hartono is the CEO of GDP Venture, the Jakarta-based venture arm of Indonesia’s Djarum Group. Aptera didn’t say which country the car is going to, what he paid for it, or when it will actually be handed over.
In the release, Hartono said Aptera is a fit for people who want to “minimize their energy consumption without compromising the ability to travel long distances.” Co-CEO Chris Anthony called it “the moment our team has worked toward for years” and said the company is working to finish more vehicles for early customers as soon as possible.
No number was given for how many more.
Where Aptera actually stands
The timing is interesting. Just seven weeks ago, Aptera cut its estimated cost to start production to about $25 million , down from $40 to $45 million, and said the first 40 production vehicles would start building by the end of 2026, with customer deliveries in early 2027 “subject to financing.”
Its Q3 report last week didn’t change that picture much. Aptera ended September with $9.2 million in cash, and $4.1 million of that is refundable reservation fees. It lost $14 million in the quarter, and its own filing says substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern “has not been alleviated.”
On November 10, it priced a $6 million registered direct offering at $1.75 per share. SEV closed at $1.67 on Tuesday, with a 52-week high of $7.
The solar side of the pitch holds up better. In August, TÜV Rheinland measured 4.23 to 4.75 kWh per day going into the battery from the car’s integrated panels in Carlsbad, which works out to roughly 40 miles of daily driving. But that conversion relies on Aptera’s 100 Wh/mile efficiency target, and today’s release itself notes that figure isn’t yet confirmed for production vehicles.
The release’s risk factors are also worth reading. They list export, import, certification and registration requirements, state dealer licensing, single-source suppliers, and whether reservations will convert into binding orders. Shipping car No. 1 to an investor overseas sidesteps most of those for now.
Electrek’s Take
Credit where it’s due. Aptera has a finished car built to a customer’s spec, which is more than Lightyear or Sono Motors ever got to before they ran out of money. We’ve followed this company since it came back in 2019, and plenty of people (us included, at times) didn’t think we’d see this day.
But I have to be honest, this looks more symbolic than like the start of a production ramp. This is a single vehicle, built before Aptera has raised the money it says it needs for series production, and it went to the person who put the most money into the company. That’s a thank-you and a good press release ahead of what will likely be another raise. It doesn’t tell us much about Aptera’s ability to build cars at a cost that works.
The real test is still the first 40 cars, and whether they reach regular reservation holders in the US. Aptera says it needs about $25 million to get there. It has $9.2 million, $4.1 million of which customers can ask back for, and it’s raising money at under $2 a share, which means a lot of dilution for every dollar.
We want this to work. Ultra-efficient cars are the only way vehicle-integrated solar makes sense, and Aptera is the last serious attempt standing. So can it fund those 40 cars before the cash runs out?

AdventHealth took the No. 1 spot in Gartner ’s Healthcare Supply Chain Top 25 for the third straight year. The health system earned a composite score of 8.06 in the 2026 ranking, ahead of Stanford Medicine at 7.45 and Bon Secours Mercy Health at 7.33.
What’s Related
The top four held their places from last year, with Corewell Health again at No. 4. Northwestern Medicine climbed four spots to No. 5, while Kaiser Permanente debuted at No. 6. Houston Methodist also made its first appearance at No. 24.
Elsewhere on the list, Mass General Brigham rose from No. 25 to No. 14, and Johns Hopkins Medicine moved from No. 21 to No. 15. Gartner also recognized Mayo Clinic, Intermountain Health, and Cleveland Clinic in its Masters category, which requires a top-five composite score in at least seven of the past 10 years. Mayo Clinic and Intermountain Health earned that designation for the ninth year in a row, and Cleveland Clinic earned it for the third time.
RELATED: Top 25 Healthcare Supply Chain Rankings for 2025
Behind the rankings
Gartner’s annual ranking, now in its 18th year, evaluates U.S. health systems. Gartner analysts’ assessments and peer opinions each account for 25% of the composite score. Patient care quality makes up 20%, bond ratings 15%, environmental, social, and governance measures 10%, and risk management 5%.
The published scores are rounded to two decimal places, and Gartner uses the underlying scores to set the order. That’s why NewYork-Presbyterian ranks No. 21, and UPMC ranks No. 22 even though both show a score of 4.66.
What the top-ranked systems are doing
Gartner found that leading health systems are giving doctors and other clinical staff a bigger say in which products they buy and use. Some are appointing medical directors to their supply chain teams. Others are linking procedure supply lists to electronic health records to cut waste and reduce variation in what clinicians use.
Health systems are also setting up inventory hubs and looking further down their supply chains for signs of disruption . Gartner found that some are pairing AI tools that flag supply risks with lists of substitutes clinicians have already approved. Health systems are also using AI in areas such as contract management and disruption monitoring.

Takata PSAN Airbag Inflator Saga Returns With 314,000-Vehicle Toyota and Lexus Recall in the US
11 photos
Photo: Toyota
The most popular Japanese manufacturer in the US market is recalling a whopping 314,029 vehicles fitted with potentially dangerous Takata passenger airbag inflators. Toyota Motor North America hasn't received any reports of ruptures involving this group of inflators, but nevertheless, these inflators are nearing the end of their operational lifespan.
Given the aforementioned, TMNA does not intend to wait for the propellant to degrade beyond safe combustion parameters. Iffy propellant could turn a life-saving airbag deployment into an explosion, risking shrapnel projection throughout the cabin. As of this writing, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has confirmed 28 deaths in the United States of America caused by exploding Takata inflators.
NHTSA campaign 26V748, which is listed under four numbers by Toyota Motor North America, covers both Toyota and Lexus vehicles produced between model years 2002 and 2017. The manufacturer's recall numbers are 26TB25, 26TA25, 26LB11, and 26LA11. The Corolla accounts for most of the affected population, and it's understandable why.
Between the sedan and pricier hatchback, the Corolla moved 248,088 units in the United States last year, making it the 11th best-selling nameplate in the country. The Camry sold even more units, with TMNA listing 316,185 for the analyzed 12-month period in the US market.
Subject compact sedans and hatchbacks were produced for model years 2003 through 2008 to the tune of 232,174 vehicles. Otherwise put, the Corolla accounts for nearly three-quarters of the total population. The 4Runner follows suit with 35,949 units from 2016 to 2017, along with 25,174 units of the 2005 to 2006 model year Tundra pickup truck.
Photo: Toyota An estimated 10,736 examples of the 2005 through 2007 Sequoia are being recalled as well, while Lexus contributes 8,931 units of the 2017 model year GX 460, an estimated 1,064 of the 2002 to 2010 SC 430, and one 2011 model year IS 250. Seriously, one vehicle only! The lone IS compact luxury sedan was manufactured on March 1, 2011, in Japan.
Per the Part 573 filing with the federal watchdog, Toyota Motor North America is targeting inflators installed either as original equipment or replaced under a prior recall. Newer inflators have more service life remaining, yet all of them continue to be monitored by the Japanese automaker. 73980-24130 and 73980-24140 are the part numbers of the subject inflators.
Said inflators feature phase-stabilized ammonium nitrate, otherwise known as PSAN, as their propellant. As you already know since the Takata airbag inflator scandal was all over the news, the chemistry can deteriorate after exposure to high absolute humidity and elevated temperatures. Repeated temperature changes can degrade the propellant as well.
These inflators pose a safety risk because bad propellant burns too violently during airbag deployment. The sealed metal cartridge inside the airbag module, namely the part that holds the propellant, is the part that may shatter and create lots of sharp metal fragments. Blasting outward through the fabric of the airbag, this shrapnel is very dangerous indeed.
Toyota and Lexus dealers nationwide will replace suspect front passenger inflators or complete airbag assemblies, depending on the vehicle, at no charge to affected customers. Notification letters should arrive in the period from December 28, 2026, through January 11, 2027.

After more than nine years in production, Lexus finally pulled the plug on the LC a few months ago, as the final copy rolled off the line in August 2026 at the Toyota City (Motomachi) factory in Japan.
Nevertheless, despite being old, this model hasn’t really started to show its age, has it? And for what it’s worth, it remains one of the best-looking premium grand tourers in the modern era. The average market price today spans from roughly $80,000 to over $100,000 in the United States of America. Some examples can reach up to $150,000, whereas others can drop below the $60,000 mark.
Paying in the region of $60K, sometimes less, would get you a Lexus LC from an early model year that has over 50,000 miles (80,000 km) on the odo. Later model years that have not seen that much action easily break into the six-digit territory . So, where does the pictured car fit? Well, it’s a 2022 model year that had 18,700 miles (30,100 km) under its belt at the time of cataloging, and that makes it an average example.
The vinyl exterior accents in the same tone as the cockpit may not be to everyone’s liking. This is an LC 500 Coupe, meaning that it packs a 5.0-liter naturally aspirated V8. The engine produced 471 hp (477 ps/351 kW) and 398 pound-feet (540 Nm) of torque when the car was new, channeling everything to the rear wheels via a 10-speed automatic transmission. This model hit 60 mph (97 kph) in 4.4 seconds, and needed over 13 seconds to complete the standing quarter mile.
Photo: Cars&Bids Some of the gear mentioned in the listing includes the All-Weather Package, Bespoke Build Package, 21-inch wheels, carbon fiber roof, and adaptive variable suspension. This Lexus LC 500 Coupe also features a heated steering wheel, heated, ventilated, and power-adjustable front sports seats, a head-up display, and a premium surround sound system from Mark Levinson, among other things.
There is a crack in front of the right front wheel, another one in front of the left rear wheel, an it looks like this machine needs an evaporator core service, the listing reveals. It had its 20,000-mile (32,186 km) service performed in August 2026, and one year before, it had its engine oil and filter changed, an alignment performed, and the cabin air filter, wipers, and key battery replaced.
The seller bought it in January 2024, and they recently put it up for grabs on Cars&Bids. The online auction ended on November 18, 2026, and with the reserve not being met, this machine failed to sell. The highest bid was $87,500, and if you believe that this Lexus LC is worth more, and you actually want it, then you should reach out to the seller here on the quoted website.

GTA 6 Gets Honored For the Worldwide Release By Everyone, Including the Aftermarket and CGI Realms
11 photos
Photo: Vossen / 1016Industries / Instagram
Everyone seems to be in love with Rockstar Games' new Grand Theft Auto VI, despite waiting for 13 years since the previous release came live. It seems that at least this time around “a bit” of waiting only enhanced the love affair.
This week has been riddled with bombshells, one after another. Early on, we found out that Amazon and Jeff Bezos decided at the last minute that Robert Pattinson – despite being 40 and already an established star in Hollywood – is the right choice for James Bond going forward; Anthropic just had its IPO on the same day that Rockstar unleashed GTA VI upon the world, and there’s also the ongoing 2026 LA Auto Show trying to compete for our attention.
The latter was shaping up to be a rather unimportant entry this year, with only the Rivian R2 and the all-new eighth-generation Hyundai Elantra making the headlines ahead of the press day. But then Chrysler also launched new goodies for the Pacifica, and Lamborghini dropped the teased surprise: its brand-new 907-hp Lamborghini Temerario Spyder was unveiled in Los Angeles, complete with a very cool vertical-hiding hardtop roof mechanism that actually enhances handling because it lowers the car’s center of gravity.
But the automotive world also decided to pay tribute to the GTA 6 (VI) release in its own way – people showed the loading screens ahead of the global release while aftermarket outlets prepared cool stuff with custom vehicles.
For example, Vossen was on point with a couple of rides – Miami recently embraced its Vice City alter ego in conjunction with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI by recreating the game’s iconic landmarks and art style. Here’s a Ram 2500 HD plastered with the murals and the Vice City sign, rocking a set of 26-inch Vossen GNX-06 in Miami White – while the entire truck is also wrapped in Xpel’s Stealth PPF.

By: Northern Miner Staff November 19, 2026
The first United States auction of deep-sea mineral leases remained on the federal schedule for noon Eastern time Thursday after a judge threw out the fisheries agency’s sign-off for the sale off American Samoa. The Marine Minerals Administration is offering two tracts covering 31.5 million acres of Pacific seabed under leases with an initial term of 20 years. Bidding is to open at $3 million (C$4.3 million) per tract in Thousand Oaks, Calif., according to the federal sale notice . “Plans for deep seabed mining must assess and prevent harm to endangered species, many of which are sacred to the Samoan people,” Elora Raymond, co-founder of community group Faʻasao Amerika Samoa, said in a statement released by Earthjustice on Tuesday. District Judge Jill Otake ruled Monday in Hawaii that the National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act by considering only the effects of the sale and preliminary surveys on protected species. The agency also had to consider the exploration and mining that could follow, she ruled. The order set aside the fisheries agency’s approval letter.
Impossible request
The leases cover metals in nodules and iron-manganese crusts on the seabed. A lease would allow preliminary work such as mapping. A successful bidder would need separate approvals and environmental reviews before more advanced exploration, testing or commercial mining, the administration said. The leasing process began with an April 2025 request from seabed developer Impossible Metals. Later that month, President Donald Trump directed federal agencies to speed up offshore mineral development to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. American Samoa’s governor has asked Washington to share proceeds from bids, rents and royalties with the territory. The Marine Minerals Administration said it would need new legal authority to share those revenues. The agency has also proposed a sale near the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam. That proposal faces a similar challenge to the fisheries agency’s review, Otake noted in her ruling.

U.S. Air Force Capt. Daniel Lee, left, and Maj. Matthew Presutti, 13th Fighter Squadron F-35 pilots, use F-35 Emulated Non-Operational Flight Program Interoperability Experience simulators in support of VALIANT SHIELD 2026 at Misawa Air Base, Japan, June 30, 2026. (U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Patrick Boyle.)
Defending the US territory of Guam against a peer threat air-and-missile (AMD) attack would require the Joint Force to fight as a single force in a battlespace where their weapons, sensors, and command and control systems were never designed to operate together. Coordinating Patriot, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD), Aegis, and fighter aircraft against simultaneous threats is an obstacle that can’t be overcome by training each service separately.
That reality is driving a new approach to live, virtual, and constructive (LVC) training that inserts simulated threats, fifth-generation fighters, and autonomous aircraft directly into the operational networks that warfighters would use in real combat.
The objective is to provide joint forces standalone training exercises that enable them to train more realistically in their own events, while allowing a seamless transition to large scale, Joint, multi-national, and/or multi-security readiness exercises at both the operational and tactical levels of war.
Through US Indo-Pacific Command’s Pacific Multi-Domain Training and Experimentation Capability (PMTEC) program, CAE is demonstrating how LVC is supporting joint AMD, the integration of collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) with F-35s, and operations in contested environments.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is a key element in this type of training and tackles the challenge of the time and manpower expenditures required to build complex, realistic exercises necessary to truly recreate the potential battlespace.
U.S. Air Force Capt. Daniel Lee, 13th Fighter Squadron F-35 pilot, uses an F-35 Emulated Non-Operational Flight Program Interoperability Experience simulator in support of VALIANT SHIELD 2026 at Misawa Air Base, Japan, June 30, 2026. (U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Patrick Boyle.)
Guam as a joint training environment
Guam’s airfields, naval facilities, and logistics infrastructure make it a critical military hub in any potential conflict in the Indo-Pacific region. Its concentrated geography also creates an unusually difficult air-defense problem.
Traditionally, each service has trained largely within its own operational responsibilities. But defending Guam demands a common understanding of the threat, shared tactics, and the ability to coordinate engagements across service boundaries. Operators need to know not only how their own systems will respond, but how those actions affect the rest of the joint force.
“A common execution error seen in the occasional joint exercises is the duplication of targeting across services. The difficulty of doing multiple exercises means these lessons get relearned as units and personnel rotate out before being able to train again in a complex scenario,” said Matthew Martin, CAE’s lead for LVC, noting that the PMTEC program addresses that problem by bringing simulations into operational command and control networks rather than building separate systems dedicated to training.
“Enabling the ease of joint training from home station, interconnecting units across vast distances, will allow our skilled warfighters to tackle these errors and transform them into lessons applied, increasing lethality and survivability.”
During Valiant Shield, for example, CAE established a simulation cell at Andersen Air Force Base on Guam and connected it to the mission network supporting the island’s regional air-defense operations. The exercise generated simulated ballistic and cruise missiles, red aircraft, and friendly forces, feeding that information into command and control systems used by the different services.
The result was a common threat picture that Army, Navy, and Air Force operators could use to coordinate engagements against a sophisticated adversary while working through the systems and procedures they would employ in combat.
The exercise also addressed something equally important: the organizational differences that technology alone cannot resolve. Said Martin: “This was an ideal location where Army, Navy, and Air Force air defenders can train together as a joint team against that sophisticated peer threat.”
Army air-defense personnel participated in Air Force-style tactical debriefings, while Air Force battle managers worked directly with Army operators to coordinate airspace. Those interactions revealed differences in Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) that could complicate operations during an actual attack.
The experience reinforced an important detail about joint training. Connecting systems provide the technical foundation, but the ability to operate as a coordinated force depends on developing common TTPs and clear communication about how the services make decisions.
Bringing fifth-generation fighters and CCA into the fight
Valiant Shield also demonstrated how geographically dispersed forces could participate in the same mission environment. CAE connected F-35 simulators at Misawa Air Base in Japan to the Guam exercise, allowing pilots to conduct defensive operations guided by Air Force controllers thousands of miles away.
The exercise went further by incorporating CCA into a joint operational scenario, giving warfighters an opportunity to begin developing tactics for platforms that are still being tested and fielded. Rather than waiting for CCA to become widely available, CAE integrated the Air Force autonomy tools into the environment and injected capabilities from its CCA Academy in Texas into the exercise.
These included simulated aircraft, autonomy software associated with the Air Force’s Autonomy Government Reference Architecture, and the control interfaces that fighter pilots would use to supervise autonomous teammates. A live MQ-28 operating near Guam also participated, enabling interaction between live and virtual CCA capabilities.
That integration matters because the challenge is not simply making autonomous aircraft fly or communicate with crewed fighters. It is determining how those aircraft will be employed during complex missions, what tasks they should perform, and how much control human operators should retain.
“CCAs will undoubtedly be a permanent fixture in future representative LVC mission exercises,” said Dr. Brian Stensrud, CAE’s Technical Fellow for Artificial Intelligence, noting that this necessitates understanding the human side of autonomy.
During Valiant Shield, CAE equipped F-35 pilots and air-battle managers with biometric monitoring devices, collecting physiological indicators and using cognitive classifiers designed to assess workload, situational awareness, and trust in autonomous systems.
“If the platform is completely autonomous and you have no visibility into how it’s functioning or how it’s making its decisions, then the trust level becomes very low,” Martin said, adding that the assessments are intended to help identify the balance between operator control and machine independence, providing feedback for the development of autonomous capabilities and their interfaces.
Using AI to create more realistic exercises with less manpower
The expanding scope of joint LVC training creates another challenge: the effort required to build and operate increasingly complex exercises. Every additional service, weapons system, sensor, and autonomous platform brings new requirements for simulation models, data integration, cybersecurity, and coordination. Preparing a large event can consume substantial time and manpower before operators ever begin training.
CAE is investing in an integrated mission environment intended to automate much of that work and make sophisticated LVC exercises easier to assemble, execute, and repeat. The goal is to use AI to translate a commander’s training objectives into an executable exercise, help select simulation tools, configure data sources, connect systems, and generate the forces and conditions needed for the scenario.
“We’re trying to close that loop with AI and automation, rather than relying on dozens of people involved in making it all happen,” Stensrud said.
Artificial intelligence also offers a way to make opposing forces more representative of real-world adversaries. Traditional constructive simulations often rely on scripted behaviors that require extensive preparation and limit how realistically the opposition can respond when conditions change.
AI-generated behavior can make simulated adversaries more dynamic and unpredictable, forcing operators to adapt rather than repeatedly train against predetermined actions.
The same approach applies to intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance training. Analysts need realistic sensor data and adversary activity to practice detecting threats, recognizing patterns, and developing assessments. AI-generated behavior, combined with simulated sensor outputs, can create more representative conditions without scripting every action.
For warfighters, the benefit is twofold: exercises can reflect a wider range of threats, while the time and manpower required to prepare them can be reduced. That could make complex joint training more practical as a recurring and more realistic capability rather than an occasional large-scale event.
Connecting training to operational networks
Making LVC available across the Pacific depends on more than just realistic simulations and AI. The underlying infrastructure must connect those capabilities to operational networks securely and reliably.
The U.S. Air Force’s Simulator Common Architecture Requirements and Standards (SCARS) program provides a foundation for that integration. Its cloud-based architecture supports cybersecurity, software updates, and the distribution of authoritative simulation data across training systems.
CAE is leveraging the SCARS architecture through the Pacific training program, hosting simulation tools within a cybersecure environment and connecting them to classified mission networks. That allows simulated threats and friendly forces to appear in operational command and control systems without constructing separate networks for every exercise. It also supports updating threat and weapons models as new capabilities and intelligence become available.
The next challenge is extending that common environment across geographically dispersed forces and allied partners.
During the US-Japan bi-lateral exercise Keen Sword in Japan, CAE expanded the capability to include Japanese air controllers, US and Japanese pilots operating F-35 simulators, and live aircraft. Link 16 connectivity and operational communications enabled virtual and live participants to train together as an allied force.
Further expansion planned for Resolute Forces Pacific 2027 this coming spring will connect locations in Japan, Guam, and Hawaii into a common air-defense environment.
That will allow warfighters to practice distributed command and control, including transferring responsibilities between command centers if an installation is attacked, damaged, or unable to communicate.
The operational implications extend beyond training personnel on their individual systems. Commanders could use the same environment to test plans, evaluate alternative courses of action, identify weaknesses, and rehearse missions before execution.
“Ultimately, that can become not just a training tool,” said Martin. “It can become a true operational capability by enabling opportunities like mission rehearsal.”
Making that vision practical will require both the integration demonstrated during recent Pacific exercises and the automation needed to generate sophisticated scenarios without extensive manual preparation.
For the military, it offers a way to prepare distributed forces for operations that cannot be adequately rehearsed through separate service training systems. For CAE, the effort brings together joint LVC integration, autonomous systems training, and AI-driven exercise development.
That would give commanders a means to refine operational plans, test how forces work together, and prepare for contested operations using the same systems they would depend on when the fight starts.

A strike could disrupt cargo operations at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach from Saturday, after the latest contract negotiations between employers and port security workers ended without agreement.
The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA), which represents shipping lines and terminal operators, warned yesterday that a walkout was a real possibility after talks with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 broke down on Tuesday – each side blaming the other for the lack of progress.
Local 26 represents approximately 250 watchmen responsible for security duties, including checking credentials at terminal entrances and conducting patrols.
Although they account for only around 2% of the ILWU workforce at the two ports, a strike could have significant consequences for cargo movements. According to the PMA, approximately 85% of Long Beach’s cargo and 33% of LA’s is handled at the terminals where Local 26 members work.
Plus, the association warned that thousands of other ILWU workers, including longshore staff, marine clerks, and foremen, could refuse to cross picket lines, potentially bringing operations to a halt.
Yesterday, the PMA claimed the union had made little progress towards accepting its proposals and was unwilling to extend the current contract beyond 12:01 am on 21 November.
Its offer included a one-time $3,200 bonus and wage increases that would bring average annual earnings for full-time watchmen to $198,000, alongside employer-funded healthcare and improved pension benefits.
However, Local 26 president Luisa Graetz challenged the employers’ version of events. She told Seatrade Maritime News that the union had submitted a counterproposal, but employers had refused to respond. She also disputed the accuracy of the wage figures presented by the PMA.
Negotiations have been ongoing for more than a year, with the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service assisting in efforts to reach an agreement.
The latest breakdown could come as a shock to many, after the two parties had previously agreed to several contract extensions to temporarily avert the threat of industrial action, most recently extending negotiations until 20 November.
The PMA also warned that a strike could have wide consequences for the US supply chain, affecting truck and rail movements, warehousing, and businesses dependent on imports and exports.
The association cited an economic analysis by maritime economist Dr John Martin, which estimated that the terminals concerned last year supported nearly 4.2 million jobs nationwide and generated $885bn in economic activity.
Despite the threat of industrial action, negotiations are not over. Both parties are scheduled to return to the bargaining table tomorrow, leaving open the possibility of a last-minute agreement or further extension.

Future Artemis Spacesuit Gets Sortie Twin, ISS Test Mission Being Planned
10 photos
Photo: Axiom Space
With all the things that are happening with the Artemis Moon exploration program, from the shift to the creation of a lunar base to the upcoming Artemis II mission, I kind of lost sight of the fact that a lot of these upcoming efforts will require a brand-new spacesuit to be realized. Luckily, those working on this new tech keep us updated from time to time.
That would be private space company Axiom , whose Extravehicular Mobility Unit (AxEMU) just reached a major milestone in its development: it passed the critical design review (CDR) and is now ready to move into production and qualification testing.
The company made the first steps toward this milestone in the summer of last year, when it delivered the first components to NASA. Since then, it has been hard at work testing everything, including components, engineering, and flight support equipment.
Up next, Axiom will start qualification testing, which requires it to perform, among other things, environmental, vibration, and life-cycle testing. If all goes well here, the path to certification is open.
Axiom plans to have the pressure garment and portable life support system ready by early next year, as it moves to performing a real-world demonstration of the suit on the International Space Station (ISS) at a yet undisclosed time.
Somewhat behind closed doors, the private space company seems to have been working on what may very well be considered a scaled-down version of the suit. They call it the Sortie suit, or AxEMU-S1, and it has been imagined for use during short-duration lunar surface excursions.
Meant to support the early crewed Artemis missions to the Moon starting in 2028, it uses certified AxEMU components, meaning Axiom will be capable of producing it in parallel to the main suit.
The suits are part of NASA's Exploration Extravehicular Mobility Unit (xEMU) program, which kicked off back in 2019 as a means to come up with the first major spacesuit redesign since the 1980s.
When ready, the protective hardware will be able to withstand the thermal extremes on the Moon (between minus 250 degrees Fahrenheit in the shade and up to 250 degrees in the sun) and survive micrometeoroid impact.
NASA also requested that the suit have resistance to the abrasive lunar dust to avoid the issues experienced during the Apollo program – back then, exposure to the lunar dust ate entire layers. Unlike existing designs, which use snoopy cap headsets for comms, the new suit will also be equipped with voice-activated microphones.
Although Axiom is the main suit supplier for the Artemis missions, another company, Collins Aerospace, is working on its own design as well, derived from one that was initially intended to replace the ones currently in use on the ISS. Sadly, Collins hasn't updated us on how things are going on this front in a very long time.

By Ian Putzger Americas correspondent
19 November 2026
Mexican cargo airlines are still facing longer waits for US approval of cross-border charter flights, even after Washington lifted restrictions on passenger services from Mexico City to the US last month.
In October 2025, the US sanctioned Mexican carriers in protest over their government’s decision in 2023 to ban freighters from Mexico City’s Benito Juarez Airport (AICM) and curtail take-off slots at the chronically congested airport, steps Washington deemed a violation of the aviation bilateral agreement between the two countries.
Faced with further sanctions and a possible downgrading of its aviation security rating, the Mexican government returned slots taken from US carriers and agreed to allow freighters to return to AICM when operations were not congested.
Amacargo, the Mexico cargo agents’ organisation, welcomed the US lifting its restrictions, calling it a direct impulse to air cargo to strengthen capacity and connectivity with the US market. It noted that airfreight volumes of electronic components and equipment had risen by 40% this year and expressed hopes for stronger connections to key US markets like Los Angeles, Chicago, New York, and Miami.
However, charters, which account for a significant portion of cross-border airfreight traffic, continue to face extended approval times, confirmed Robert Van De Weg, CEO of Mexican cargo airline mas. He expressed confidence that the Mexican and US governments would “work this out”, adding that “the market is very strong right now”.
Statistics from Mexico’s Civil Aviation Agency (AFAC) for the first nine months of the year show 5.5% year-on-year growth in the nation’s air cargo volume, led by Felipe Angeles International Airport (AIFA), the Mexican capital’s designated freighter gateway, which reported an increase of 7.2%, to 313,860 tons.
AICM’s throughput rose 2.3%, to 188,418 tons. Opening it again to freighter operators does not seem likely to spur a surge in tonnage, though. To begin with, AFAC has indicated that windows for freighter operations would be between 11.30pm and 12.30am, and from 5am to 6am.
Moreover, AICM director general Juan José Padilla Olmos told Mexican media in late October that none of the freighter operators now using AIFA had signalled any intention to return to AICM. According to Peter Cerdá, executive director and CEO of the Latin American and Caribbean Air Transport Association, a few cargo carriers are interested in a switch, but the majority like the better infrastructure and ease of obtaining landing slots at AIFA.
Passenger airlines are gearing up for expansion. Delta and joint-venture partner Aeromexico have announced new routes from Mexico City to Nashville, New Orleans, and San Juan next June.
Mas is also expanding its network, but not to the US this year. In December, it will launch weekly flights to Edmonton, a service anchored by Fresh Direct Produce, one of Canada’s leading importers of fresh produce. The flight will also carry an array of other commodities, including auto parts, pharmaceuticals, tech products, agricultural equipment, and flowers.
Mr Van De Weg intends to open a second route to the US in 2027, as he expects to add at least one converted A330 freighter to the mas fleet in the coming year.

Alliance Ground International’s (AGI) dispute with airport workers’ union 32BJ SEIU has widened to holiday pay, the union saying workers at New York’s JFK Airport have complained that the cargo handler failed to pay them all they were owed.
The complaints are the latest development in a months-long campaign that has seen the union take workers’ safety allegations to federal regulators, as well as a protest outside TIACA’s Air Cargo Forum in Miami last month.
AGI has pushed back on the safety allegations, citing its procedures for equipment inspections, maintenance, and training, and saying an OSHA inspection does not establish a violation.
The handler has accused SEIU of using “false and misleading claims” to pressure it into recognising the union. Indeed, AGI sued SEIU and its Local 32BJ in Florida’s state court in July and sought a preliminary injunction, alleging the campaign had cost it more than $19.8m in annual airline business, including contracts with IAG carriers and Singapore Airlines. The union called the suit “meritless”, and the case remains open.
32BJ said workers had filed the holiday-pay complaints with the New York State Department of Labor, under the state’s Healthy Terminals Act. The union estimates workers could be owed hundreds of thousands of dollars in back pay and scheduled a rally at JFK today. It did not say how many workers had complained or how it calculated the estimate.
Freddie Robles, an AGI security officer at JFK, said he worked 40 hours a week on the overnight shift and had worked on seven holidays this year, from New Year’s Day to Veterans Day.
“AGI still has not paid me all the holiday pay I’m owed,” he said in a statement issued by the union. “When my paycheck comes up short, my entire life gets thrown off balance.”
New York’s Department of Labor says covered workers – some 700 AGI staff at JFK and LaGuardia, according to the union – are entitled to at least 12 paid holidays a year.
In May, 32BJ said, it had filed federal safety complaints on behalf of 21 AGI workers at JFK and LaGuardia, alleging faulty tug brakes, inadequate training, and insufficient heat protection. AGI told The Loadstar it cooperates fully with OSHA and declined to discuss pending investigations.
At TIACA’s Air Cargo Forum in Miami last month, AGI chief executive Jared Azcuy said the company had added AI to its warehouse cameras in a move to boost safety.
“Our first focus was really on safety, and we put AI technology on top of all our existing cameras,” he told a conference panel. “It wasn’t meant to be punitive. It was meant to be coaching them and getting the best safety environment out of the team.”
AGI told The Loadstar it used Voxel’s computer vision system at all its warehouses, software that analyses CCTV footage around the clock and flags hazards such as forklifts passing too close to pedestrians, unsafe lifting, spills, and missing protective equipment. The company says it uses clips to train new hires, refresh existing staff’s training, and talk through specific incidents with workers.
It added that the system “does not replace mechanical inspections, preventive maintenance, or the physical examination of equipment for defects such as faulty brakes or seat belts”. Staff are expected to check equipment before use, report faults, and take unsafe equipment out of service, AGI said.
AGI’s annual safety report says recordable injuries at its JFK operation fell 91% over one year after it introduced Voxel, while the frequency of workers’ compensation claims fell 36%. Voxel’s own case study noted: “AGI’s JFK operation had an elevated injury rate, serious injury potential from falls and powered industrial trucks, high turnover, 24-hour operation with limited visibility, and high rates of cargo damage.
“But they also had a new leader who was motivated to build a new safety culture from the ground up. Voxel gave them the tools to do that… the results have been excellent so far.”

Former Jeremy Clarkson-Owned Ferrari F355 GTS Sells for Double the Auction Estimate
11 photos
Photo: Iconic Auctioneers
If there was need for further proof that being a celebrity pays off, then what follows is exactly that: a Ferrari F355 GTS bought new by Jeremy Clarkson, one of the most iconic figures in television, just sold for more than twice the money the guy selling it was hoping for.
Truth be told, the huge amount of cash spent on it (more on that in a bit) didn't go to Clarkson himself, as the man has long parted ways with the car, giving it as a prize to a reader of his Sunday Times columns some 26 years ago.
Since that time, it probably exchanged hands several times, and the current owner listed it for sale during the Iconic Auctioneers’ NEC Classic Motor Show Sales event last week. Someone bought it and set a live auction world record in the process.
Back when it announced the sale of the Rosso Corsa Prancing Horse , Iconic Auctioneers estimated it would go for between £200,000 and £250,000 (that's $263,000 to $329,000). Because the right guy was in the house when the Italian beauty went under the hammer, it ended up selling for £405,000 ($533,000), which is more than double the lower estimate.
We don't know who the buyer of the Ferrari is, but we do know what they got themselves earlier this month: a car packing its original V8 engine and six-speed manual, the factory-installed carbon-backed sports seats in Crema leather, and even the original order correspondence and the Warranty Card that proves the TV star was the vehicle's first owner.
With 15,200 miles (24,462 km) on the odometer, chassis number ZFFXR42C000106175 also comes complete with the original tool kit, red carpets, and the removable targa roof that makes this thing a true GTS.
In the time that has passed since it was purchased by Clarkson, the Ferrari was subjected to some restoration and repair work by its subsequent owners. That includes cosmetic tweaks, both inside and outside, steering rack repairs, and a cambelt replacement.
Bought new by Clarkson but no longer in his possession, the 1996 Ferrari F355 GTS didn't make the star any actual money this time. But the man did have his own vehicles listed for sale during the Iconic Auctioneers event, and they all lived up to their hype.
No less than three Clarkson-owned cars went under the hammer, achieving a combined £160,312 (around $211,000). First up is the 1982 Lancia Montecarlo Spider, the last car the man drove in The Grand Tour, which snatched £69,187 ($91,000), a live auction record as well.
The rest of the money comes from Clarkson also selling his 1983 Alfa Romeo GTV6 from The Grand Tour adventure that became known as ‘Well Aged Scotch ', and the 1978 Lincoln Continental Mark V that made an appearance in The Grand Tour Presents: Lochdown, a COVID-era special filmed in Scotland.

By Alex Lennane
19 November 2026
Expeditors is rethinking its approach to acquisitions, and is already evaluating opportunities in technology, a major shift for a forwarder that has built most of its global network through organic growth.
“For the last 10 years, we have been very quiet in this zone and not looking at M&A almost in any regard. That has changed,” chief financial officer Dave Hackett told the company’s first investor day in 11 years.
“We are evaluating various things in the tech space right now,” he added, but gave no details of the opportunities under review or what form any transaction might take.
Expeditors ranked strategic transactions second among its capital allocation priorities, behind organic investment and ahead of returning excess cash to shareholders.
The prospect of M&A prompted an analyst to ask how Expeditors would integrate another business while preserving the culture its executives had spent much of the morning describing.
Each of its 173 districts runs its own profit and loss account, with district managers’ pay tied to local performance. The offices have discretion over how they serve customers and invest in their teams, within common operating standards and systems. The senior leadership team has an average tenure of 27 years. CEO Dan Wall started as a messenger, moved into air import operations, and was running the Denver district by the age of 23.
“We don’t want to change our culture. We don’t intend to change our culture,” said Mr Hackett. He pointed to technology capabilities as an example of an area where Expeditors had historically been quiet, even for smaller transactions.
Mr Wall said any deal would have to be “something that just complements what we’re already doing and doesn’t take away from everything else we built”.
Those assurances follow an unusual round of job cuts at a forwarder long known for retaining staff through downturns. In June, Expeditors notified Washington State of plans to cut about 230 jobs in its Global Technology division. The company later told investors it had never had a blanket no-layoff policy, and described the cuts as part of a technology modernisation.
At the investor day, Mr Wall said the company’s pay model helped it “avoid layoffs at the operational level” when business slowed.
He described the 1986 purchase of Pac Bridge, which took Expeditors into ocean freight, as probably its last major acquisition. A more recent deal shows how it has bought a specific capability: in 2020, Expeditors acquired Fleet Logistics’ digital platform to support Koho, its online less-than-truckload shipping service.
Expeditors gave no geographic preference for deals. Kelly Blacker, president of global geographies, cited India as a market where the company was building-out domestic road freight. She also pointed to Mexico and India as places where long-established local teams could take on more business as manufacturing shifted.
Mr Hackett said Expeditors could borrow to fund an acquisition, and could cut back share buybacks to pay down debt if leverage rose above the level it wanted to carry long-term. Asked whether that meant it could be looking at a deal worth $1bn or more, he replied: “Not suggesting that.
“We do not have a strategy to grow through M&A,” he said. “We have a strategy to monitor M&A and look for strategic positioning, strategic gaps we can fill, and generate returns.”
